blocks.x: A 3,000-Year-Old Warhorse Burial and a Ramses II Tablet, Among Other Relics, Have Been Discovered in an Ancient Egyptian Fortress
New excavations in the Nile Delta offer eye-opening clues about military and residential life in the New Kingdom era

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/eaCGXzTq9CdBBl8YrDGdR_PQ8gw=/1026x684/filters:focal(750x500:751x501)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/fb/a9/fba9bff4-b78d-4c05-b896-df879dcc3f95/790562685_2226708541441523_6987418583732232031_n.jpeg

Archaeologists working within a recently discovered fortress in the Nile River Delta say they have excavated a trove of artifacts and remains that shed new light on the daily military and social cadences of ancient Egyptian society.

Recent digs at a roughly 3,000-year-old fortress—originally unearthed in 2024 within a larger site called Al-Abqaa’, or Tell Al-Abqain, in Egypt’s modern-day Beheira province—contains the remains of mudbrick houses, wells, grain silos, roads and pottery ovens used to prepare food.

The fortress, though established near the country’s western border to defend from attacks launched by neighboring armies, also harbored routine residential life. The complex was likely a thriving community during Egypt’s New Kingdom era, which lasted from 1570 B.C.E. to 1069 B.C.E. The treasures that have survived inside for millennia are just beginning to be found.

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/MjGIoJASG7YxUNzAbiOzE_f5UUU=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(640x482:641x483)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/75/eb/75eb6249-243a-4732-99f8-d355edc22992/813546241_1500608518767356_3582047783393046498_n.jpg

Among the most exciting new excavations is the 3,000-year-old grave of a young male warhorse that may have been used in battle. The horse’s skeleton was found intact, and its alabaster and limestone chariot harness was dug up nearby, indicating that the horse had been honored with a ceremonial burial, according to a statement from the Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities.

“It is an amazing find, simply because we have so few horse remains from Pharaonic Egypt,” Lonneke Delpeut, a historian at the University of Vienna, tells Live Science’s Owen Jarus. “This horse will therefore surely contribute to what we know about the use of horses in military forts, of which there are many in the region.”
Quick fact: Ancient Egyptian equines

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/CuxeJtmgtoMGZPR8qCT29zRXnJo=/fit-in/200x200/filters:no_upscale()/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/accounts/headshot/ChristianThorsberg_Headshot.png
The
Hyksos have been credited with introducing the domestic horse to ancient Egypt—and thereby to Africa—around 1600 B.C.E.

In ancient Egyptian society, horses were owned and used by royals and military elites. Instead of being ridden, they were typically paired to transport pharaohs and chariots into war. This was especially true during the New Kingdom era.

Hieroglyphs carved into temple walls at the time, according to research from the Julius Maximilian University of Würzburg, detail royals’ wartime relationship with horses and their linked iconography: King Thutmose III, for example, rode into battle against the Canaanites at Megiddo “on a chariot of fine gold, decked in his shining armor like strong-armed Horus”; his son Amenhotep II mastered horses that “did not grow tired when he took the reins, and they did not drip with sweat at a high gallop”; Thutmoseis IV was famously buried with his war chariot.

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/lRV_zhkNCfOF-EqOk9irKQaGFxc=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(800x800:801x801)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/02/1e/021e3de5-e4d7-4252-8ba3-2d335135806c/812781707_1500608558767352_4006712901112882649_n.jpg

Carolyn Willekes, a historian at Mount Royal University, in Canada, tells Live Science that Al-Abqaa’s seemingly “intentional horse burial also gives tantalizing hints about the equine-human relationship in ancient Egypt and the cultural importance of the horse.”

Other discoveries at the fortress shed further light on the region’s conflict and power hierarchy. Archaeologists also uncovered a fragment of a limestone stela depicting a bound prisoner, likely a member of a Libyan tribe, bent in a submissive position. Another stela is inscribed with the birth name, throne name and Horus name of Ramses II, while a third compares his son, Merneptah, a ruler himself, to the god Seth.

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/SceiMl7B0Apd6MLPMkuN6o42o2s=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(418x576:419x577)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/dd/17/dd178484-007b-4205-8e6d-37dbdf1db016/812342969_1500608532100688_1167415948055569865_n.jpg

Amulets, looms, jewelry and a variety of pottery vessels—made in the shape of fish, lotus flowers, crocodile scales and baboons—were also discovered in and around ancient residences, according to the Egyptian ministry. Some old crop warehouses still contained traces of unhusked grain. Further excavations are planned for the historic site.

“It is an important discovery highlighting the strategic role of Tell Al-Abqain area as a crucial military outpost on the western military road, protecting Egypt’s northwestern borders from potential invasions by Libyan tribes and sea peoples,” Mohamed Ismail Khaled, secretary-general of Egypt’s Supreme Council of Antiquities, told Ahram Online’s Nevine El-Aref in 2024.
